name: Bagchen
description: Bagchen (meaning 'Great Game' or 'Bird Game') is the national domino game of Tibet. Played with a double set of Chinese dominoes (64 tiles), it is a sophisticated trick-taking game similar to the Chinese classic Tien Gow. However, Bagchen introduces a brutal 'Scorched Earth' victory condition: winning individual tricks is merely a means to an end; the only trick that truly matters is the very last one. It involves complex 'set' leading, where players can play up to four tiles at once in coordinated formations.

history.origins: Rooted in the ancient trade routes between Tibet and China. While it shares the civil/military tile hierarchy with Chinese Tien Gow, Bagchen evolved in the monasteries and aristocrat circles of Lhasa into a distinct game with unique scoring and grouping rules.
timeline: 17th Century: Bagchen becomes a favorite pastime of the Tibetan nobility.
1950s: Tibetan diaspora brings Bagchen to India, Nepal, and the West.
Present: Still played with traditional hand-carved bone or plastic tiles in Tibetan communities worldwide.
history.cultural: Regarded as a game of high prestige. In traditional Tibetan society, a player's skill in Bagchen was seen as a reflection of their intellect and character.
history.evolution: The game shifted from a gambling-focused single-trick payout system to a more strategic session-based game where team cooperation is vital.

setup.players: 4 players. No partnerships; play is clockwise.
setup.deck: Two sets of Chinese dominoes (32 x 2 = 64). Each tile represents two dice faces.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 16 tiles. Tiles are usually arranged in 'stacks' or 'walls' before being drawn.
setup.equipment: 64 tiles, traditionally stored in a carved wooden box. A bowl for tokens/chips.

rules.objective: Win the final trick of the hand. The winner of the final trick is paid by the other players according to chips won; winning all 16 tricks wins all chips. Session may end with Gobah (five more deals), the last being Tashi Gobah.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Setup**: Tiles are stacked (wood wall). Each player draws 16 tiles. 2. **Tile Hierarchy**: Civil (Wen) has 11 ranksâ€”6-6 (Heaven) highest; Military (Wu) has 10 ranksâ€”2-4 and 1-2 (The Supreme) highest. 3. **Lead**: Winner of previous trick (or dealer on first) leads 1â€“4 tiles (single, pair, or set of 3â€“4 matching). 4. **Follow**: Others must play the same number of tiles. To win the trick, beat every tile in the lead with higher-ranking tiles of the same suit. 5. **Bury**: If you cannot beat the lead, bury tiles face down (waste). 6. **Final Trick**: Winning the 16th trick scores 1 point (2 if won with a Supreme set). First team to target (11 or 21) wins.
keyRules: No Trump suit: The Civil/Military distinction acts as a dual-suit system.
Waste Tiles: Tiles buried face down cannot be retrieved or inspected.
Dealer rotation only happens if the non-dealing team wins the final trick.
Players can lead singles, pairs, or sets of 3â€“4 tiles of matching rank or suit.

strategy.basic: Save your big tiles (6-6, 1-1, 4-4) for the end. It doesn't matter if you lose the first 15 tricks as long as you have the highest tile for the 16th.
strategy.intermediate: Exhaust the opponent's 'Civil' suit early. If you have many Military tiles, lead them to force out your opponents' big Civil tiles so they can't use them to win the final trick.
strategy.advanced: Set Detection: If an opponent leads a 'Double Pair', they are signaling they have a deep hand. You must decide whether to challenge them now or save your tiles to 'bury' theirs later.
tips: In Bagchen, 'The Supreme' (2-4 / 1-2) is the ultimate trap. Use it to win a trick that allows you to lead a set your opponent can't beat.
Communicate with your partner through your discards. If you bury a high Civil tile, it tells your partner you are 'running dry' on that suit.

variations.name: Lhasa Short Game
variations.description: A version where only 12 tricks are played (8 tiles per player) for faster sessions.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: This short game only changes deal length and number of tricks; all other rules follow the main Bagchen configuration.

scoring.description: Scoring is binary for the final trick, but cumulative for the session.

synthesis.shortDescription: Immerse yourself in Tibet's most profound strategic tradition. Bagchen is a game of extreme patience and calculated sacrifice. Navigate the complex hierarchy of Civil and Military tiles across 16 tricks, burying your losses and hoarding your power for the one moment that defines the game.
